claim: The dileucine zipper kinase (DLK) is also known as MAP3K12 in mammals.
source: The dileucine zipper kinase (DLK; also known as MAP3K12 in mammals and Wallenda (Wnd) in Drosophila) is a key regulator of diverse responses to axonal injury.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established nomenclature.

claim: The dileucine zipper kinase (DLK) is known as Wallenda (Wnd) in Drosophila.
source: The dileucine zipper kinase (DLK; also known as MAP3K12 in mammals and Wallenda (Wnd) in Drosophila) is a key regulator of diverse responses to axonal injury.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established nomenclature.

claim: DLK/Wnd is a key regulator of diverse responses to axonal injury.
source: The dileucine zipper kinase (DLK; also known as MAP3K12 in mammals and Wallenda (Wnd) in Drosophila) is a key regulator of diverse responses to axonal injury.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the literature and the study's findings.

claim: In three different populations of motoneurons, Wnd/DLK signaling becomes activated only in response to injuries that remove all synaptic terminals.
source: In three different populations of MNs, we observed the same striking result that Wnd/DLK signaling becomes activated only in response to injuries that remove all synaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from multiple MN populations.

claim: Injuries that spared even a small part of a synaptic terminal were insufficient to activate Wnd/DLK signaling.
source: Injuries that spared even a small part of a synaptic terminal were insufficient to activate Wnd/DLK signaling, despite the presence of extensive axonal degeneration.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data showing no puc-lacZ induction with spared synapses.

claim: Injuries that spared synaptic terminals did not activate Wnd/DLK signaling despite the presence of extensive axonal degeneration.
source: Injuries that spared even a small part of a synaptic terminal were insufficient to activate Wnd/DLK signaling, despite the presence of extensive axonal degeneration.
evidence: This finding demonstrates that axonal degeneration alone is not sufficient to activate Wnd/DLK signaling.

claim: The regulation of injury-induced Wnd/DLK signaling occurs independently of the Hiw/PHR ubiquitin ligase.
source: The regulation of injury-induced Wnd/DLK signaling occurs independently of its previously known regulator, the Hiw/PHR ubiquitin ligase.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experiments in hiw mutants showing additive effects.

claim: Wnd/DLK signaling regulation is linked to the trafficking of a synapse-to-nucleus axonal cargo.
source: We propose that Wnd/DLK signaling regulation is linked to the trafficking of a synapse-to-nucleus axonal cargo and that this mechanism enables neurons to respond to impairments in synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the study's findings and previous literature on axonal transport.

claim: The mechanism of Wnd/DLK signaling regulation enables neurons to respond to impairments in synaptic connectivity.
source: We propose that Wnd/DLK signaling regulation is linked to the trafficking of a synapse-to-nucleus axonal cargo and that this mechanism enables neurons to respond to impairments in synaptic connectivity.
evidence: This is a proposed functional interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The location of damage can influence the intrinsic ability of the neuron to mount a transcriptional response to the damage.
source: While many studies have identified extrinsic factors that influence or inhibit axonal regeneration, several studies have noted that the location of damage can influence the intrinsic ability of the neuron to mount a transcriptional response to the damage (Fernandes et al., 1999; Lorenzana et al., 2015; Mason et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: Distance from the cell body affects the response to injury for long axons in the spinal cord.
source: Some studies have noted an effect of distance from the cell body for long axons in the spinal cord (Fernandes et al., 1999; Mason et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The location of injury with respect to an axonal branching point strongly influences the response.
source: Other studies have noted that the location of injury with respect to an axonal branching point also strongly influences the response (Lorenzana et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Dorsal column sensory axons show robust axonal growth when injured proximal to their bifurcation in the spinal cord, even in a strongly inhibitory environment to regeneration.
source: Even in a strongly inhibitory environment to regeneration, dorsal column sensory axons show robust axonal growth when injured proximal to their bifurcation in the spinal cord (Lorenzana et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: DLK has an essential role in the ability of damaged neurons to initiate axonal regeneration in worm and fly models.
source: These include an essential role in the ability of damaged neurons to initiate axonal regeneration in worm and fly models (Chen et al., 2011; Hammarlund et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by multiple cited studies.

claim: DLK is involved in synaptic repair and recovery following CCR5 inhibition in a stroke model.
source: These include an essential role in the ability of damaged neurons to initiate axonal regeneration in worm and fly models (Chen et al., 2011; Hammarlund et al., 2009; Stone et al., 2014; Xiong et al., 2010; Yan et al., 2009), synaptic repair and recovery following CCR5 inhibition in a stroke model (Joy et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: DLK is involved in enhanced regeneration and mechanical allodynia following PNS nerve damage in mice.
source: enhanced regeneration and mechanical allodynia following PNS nerve damage in mice (Hu et al., 2019; Wlaschin et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: DLK is required for the death of retinal ganglion cells following optic nerve damage.
source: Dichotomously, DLK is also required for the death of retinal ganglion cells following optic nerve damage (Watkins et al., 2013; Welsbie et al., 2017; Welsbie et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: DLK associates with vesicles that are physically transported in axons in mammalian and fly neurons.
source: In mammalian as well as in fly neurons, this kinase associates with vesicles that are physically transported in axons (Holland et al., 2016; Xiong et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Downstream nuclear signaling by DLK requires functional axonal transport machinery.
source: while downstream nuclear signaling requires functional axonal transport machinery (Xiong et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: DLK is considered to function as a 'sensor' of axonal damage.
source: DLK is therefore considered to function as a 'sensor' of axonal damage, whose activation can confer responses of repair or death, depending upon the cellular context (Asghari Adib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation supported by cited literature.

claim: DLK activation can confer responses of repair or death, depending upon the cellular context.
source: DLK is therefore considered to function as a 'sensor' of axonal damage, whose activation can confer responses of repair or death, depending upon the cellular context (Asghari Adib et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by cited literature.

claim: DLK signaling activation has been documented in neurons that are not mechanically damaged but have experienced some form of cellular stress.
source: A number of observations have documented DLK signaling activation in neurons that are not mechanically damaged but have experienced some form of cellular stress.
evidence: This is supported by the examples that follow in the text.

claim: DLK signaling is activated in the presence of cytoskeletal mutations.
source: These include the presence of cytoskeletal mutations (Bounoutas et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2014; Kurup et al., 2015; Valakh et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: DLK signaling is activated in the presence of chemotherapy agents known to impair axonal cytoskeleton integrity and transport.
source: and the presence of chemotherapy agents (Bhattacharya et al., 2012; DeVault et al., 2024; Valakh et al., 2015) known to impair axonal cytoskeleton integrity and transport
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: DLK activation is responsible for phenotypes associated with mutations in the unc-104/KIF1A kinesin.
source: DLK activation is also responsible for phenotypes associated with mutations in the unc-104/KIF1A kinesin (Li et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: unc-104/KIF1A is a major carrier of synaptic vesicle precursors in axons.
source: a major carrier of synaptic vesicle precursors in axons (Guedes-Dias and Holzbaur, 2019; Petzoldt, 2023)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Inhibition of DLK is protective in mouse models of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).
source: Inhibition of DLK is protective in mouse models of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease (Le Pichon et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Inhibition of DLK is protective in mouse models of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Inhibition of DLK is protective in mouse models of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease (Le Pichon et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: A shared feature of nerve injuries and stressors that disrupt axonal cytoskeleton and transport is a loss in downstream connections.
source: A shared feature of nerve injuries and stressors that disrupt axonal cytoskeleton and transport is a loss in downstream connections.
evidence: This is an observation that connects different types of injuries and stressors.

claim: The E3-ubiquitin ligase PAM/Highwire/Rpm-1/Phr1 is a conserved regulator of DLK/Wnd.
source: A conserved regulator of DLK/Wnd, the E3-ubiquitin ligase PAM/Highwire/Rpm-1/Phr1 (Collins et al., 2006; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Nakata et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: PAM/Highwire/Rpm-1/Phr1 is hypothesized to function at synaptic terminals.
source: is hypothesized to function at synaptic terminals (Abrams et al., 2008; Opperman and Grill, 2014; Xiong et al., 2012; Zhen et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The m12 (5053A)-Gal4 driver line drives expression in two single motoneurons that project closely fasciculated axons to innervate body wall muscles 26, 27, and 29.
source: The m12 (5053A)-Gal4 driver line (Ritzenthaler et al., 2000) that we have used in previous nerve injury studies (Xiong et al., 2010; Xiong and Collins, 2012), drives expression in two single MNs that project closely fasciculated axons to innervate body wall muscles 26, 27, and 29 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study and confirmed by the authors' observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The innervation pattern was previously attributed to an MN named MNSNc, which was noted to have 'two cell bodies'.
source: This pattern was previously attributed to an MN named MNSNc, which was noted to have 'two cell bodies' (Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: One MNSNc neuron innervates muscles 26 and 29, while the other innervates muscle 27.
source: We used the Bitbow2 (Li et al., 2021) multi-colored cell labeling approach to resolve the two neurons and observed an invariable pattern that one MNSNc neuron innervates muscles 26 and 29, while the other innervates muscle 27.
evidence: This is a finding from the study using Bitbow2 labeling, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MNSNc-26/29 has three collateral branches: two branches innervate muscle 26, and a single branch innervates muscle 29.
source: MNSNc-26/29 (cartooned in blue in Figure 1A) has three collateral branches: two branches innervate muscle 26, and a single branch innervates muscle 29.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: MNSNc-27 has two collateral branches that innervate muscle 27.
source: MNSNc-27 (cartooned in red in Figure 1A) has two collateral branches that innervate muscle 27
evidence: This is a finding from the study, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The two branches of MNSNc-27 most often remain together and occasionally bifurcate separately onto muscle 27.
source: these two branches most often remain together and occasionally bifurcate separately onto muscle 27 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The innervation pattern of MNSNc neurons is stereotyped across segments and animals.
source: This innervation is stereotyped across segments and animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The paired cell bodies of the MNSNc neurons are found on the lateral sides of the abdominal region of the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
source: As previously noted (Kim et al., 2009), the paired cell bodies of the MNSNc neurons are found on the lateral sides of the abdominal region of the ventral nerve cord (VNC).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study and confirmed by the authors.

claim: The MNSNc-27 cell somas are positioned more ventrally compared to the cell somas of MNSNc-26/29 in the VNC.
source: Bitbow2 expression revealed that the MNSNc-27 cell somas are positioned more ventrally compared to the cell somas of MNSNc-26/29 in the VNC (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study using Bitbow2 labeling, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Laser axotomy of the m12-Gal4 labeled neurons upstream of the synaptic branches led to a fourfold induction of puc-lacZ expression in both neurons 24 hr after injury.
source: We confirmed this is the case for MNSNc neurons; axotomy of the m12-Gal4 labeled neurons upstream of the synaptic branches led to a fourfold induction of puc-lacZ expression in both neurons 24 hr after injury
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The induction of puc-lacZ following axotomy was abolished in neurons that co-express double-stranded RNAi targeting wnd.
source: this was abolished in neurons that co-express double-stranded RNAi targeting wnd (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Nerve crush injuries to MNSNc neurons induce puc-lacZ expression.
source: Similar results were observed for nerve crush injuries (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Laser injury to single collateral branches of MNSNc-26/29 that resulted in spared synaptic branches did not induce puc-lacZ expression.
source: In contrast to axotomies that removed all synaptic branches, laser injury to single collateral branches of MNSNc-26/29, including branches innervating either muscle 26 or 29 and resulting in spared synaptic branches, did not induce puc-lacZ expression (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: Laser ablation of the anterior branch of MNSNc-27 was insufficient to activate Wnd signaling.
source: In addition, laser ablation of the anterior branch of MNSNc-27 was also insufficient to activate Wnd signaling (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: The induction of puc-lacZ did not correlate with the number of boutons that were lost or spared.
source: We note that the induction of puc-lacZ did not correlate with the number of boutons that were lost or spared.
evidence: This is an observation from the study's data.

claim: MNSNc-26/29 forms fourfold more boutons on muscle 26 (17 ± 3.8) than 29 (4 ± 1.3).
source: MNSNc-26/29 forms fourfold more boutons on muscle 26 (17 ± 3.8) than 29 (4 ± 1.3).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the study.

claim: Injuries that spared any of the branches, even the small number on muscle 29, showed equivalent puc-lacZ levels to uninjured neurons.
source: However, injuries that spared any of the branches, even the small number on muscle 29, showed equivalent puc-lacZ levels to uninjured neurons (Figure 1E; compare injury locations a, b, and c).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Laser axotomies that removed all of the synaptic branches of aCC MNs resulted in a fourfold increase in puc-LacZ levels.
source: Laser axotomies that removed all of the synaptic branches resulted in a fourfold increase in puc-LacZ levels, while injuries that left spared synaptic boutons did not induce puc-lacZ expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Injuries to aCC MNs that left spared synaptic boutons did not induce puc-lacZ expression.
source: Laser axotomies that removed all of the synaptic branches resulted in a fourfold increase in puc-LacZ levels, while injuries that left spared synaptic boutons did not induce puc-lacZ expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Even a small number of remaining boutons was sufficient to restrain the activation of puc-lacZ expression.
source: These observations suggested that even a small number of remaining boutons was sufficient to restrain the activation of puc-lacZ expression.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: None of the injured MNSNc synaptic branches were able to re-innervate the muscle.
source: Despite the small distance from the disconnected muscle, none of the injured MNSNc synaptic branches were able to re-innervate the muscle.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: MNSNc axons showed robust but misdirected axonal growth into the segmental nerve SNa following injuries in locations upstream of the synaptic branches.
source: We think this is due to an absence of axon growth-promoting cues, since MNSNc axons did show robust but misdirected axonal growth into the segmental nerve SNa following injuries in locations upstream of the synaptic branches (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: GFP-Wnd-KD was strongly induced and accumulated at the proximal stump following injuries that removed all synaptic branches.
source: GFP-Wnd-KD was strongly induced and accumulated at the proximal stump following injuries that removed all synaptic branches but was barely detectable following injuries that left spared synaptic branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: GFP-Wnd-KD was barely detectable following injuries that left spared synaptic branches.
source: GFP-Wnd-KD was strongly induced and accumulated at the proximal stump following injuries that removed all synaptic branches but was barely detectable following injuries that left spared synaptic branches (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G.

claim: The presence of spared synaptic branches affects the stability and/or trafficking of Wnd protein in injured axons.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that the presence of spared synaptic branches affects the subsequent events that occur in the injured axon. These include the stability and/or trafficking of Wnd protein in injured axons and the activation of Wnd-regulated signaling in the neuron soma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The presence of spared synaptic branches affects the activation of Wnd-regulated signaling in the neuron soma.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that the presence of spared synaptic branches affects the subsequent events that occur in the injured axon. These include the stability and/or trafficking of Wnd protein in injured axons and the activation of Wnd-regulated signaling in the neuron soma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Ventral unpaired median neurons project symmetric bifurcated axons through separate nerves to innervate multiple body wall muscles on both left and right sides of the larva.
source: A more extreme example of axonal branching is illustrated by the ventral unpaired median neurons, which project symmetric bifurcated axons through separate nerves to innervate multiple body wall muscles on both left and right sides of the larva (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Koon et al., 2011; Monastirioti et al., 1995; Vömel and Wegener, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies and illustrated in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: VUM neurons can be specifically labeled based on their expression of tyrosine decarboxylase 2 using the Tdc2-Gal4 driver.
source: VUM neurons can be specifically labeled based on their expression of tyrosine decarboxylase 2 using the Tdc2-Gal4 driver.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about labeling VUM neurons.

claim: Each abdominal segment has three VUM neurons.
source: Each abdominal segment has three VUM neurons, each of which sends a single axon dorsally which then bifurcates in the midline VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Vömel and Wegener, 2008).

claim: Each VUM neuron sends a single axon dorsally which then bifurcates in the midline VNC.
source: Each abdominal segment has three VUM neurons, each of which sends a single axon dorsally which then bifurcates in the midline VNC (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Vömel and Wegener, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study and illustrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The two bifurcations of VUM neurons project through separate nerves to symmetrically innervate both left and right halves of the larval body.
source: The two bifurcations then project through separate nerves to symmetrically innervate both left and right halves of the larval body.
evidence: This is a description of VUM neuron anatomy.

claim: puc-lacZ expression is barely detectable in uninjured VUM MNs.
source: Similarly to other MNs (Xiong et al., 2010), puc-lacZ expression is barely detectable in uninjured VUM MNs
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with previous observations.

claim: puc-lacZ is induced almost threefold at 24 hr following complete/full nerve crush injuries that damage both bifurcations and remove all synaptic connections in VUM neurons.
source: and, compared to uninjured VUM neurons, is induced almost threefold at 24 hr following complete/full nerve crush injuries that damage both bifurcations and remove all synaptic connections (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: The induction of puc-lacZ in VUM neurons following full nerve crush is abolished in VUM neurons that co-express wnd-RNAi.
source: This induction is abolished in VUM neurons that co-express wnd-RNAi (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: Injuries to nerves on a single side of the animal that left the other bifurcation intact ('half crush' injuries) did not induce puc-lacZ expression in VUM neurons.
source: In contrast to full nerve crushes, injuries to nerves on a single side of the animal that the other bifurcation was intact ('half crush' injuries) did not induce puc-lacZ expression in VUM neurons (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, shown in Figure 2C, D.

claim: Most MNs make ipsilateral and not bilateral projections.
source: Most MNs make ipsilateral and not bilateral projections
evidence: This is a general statement about MN anatomy.

claim: In 'half-crush' injuries, puc-lacZ is induced in most non-VUM MNs on the side of the crush, but is not induced in VUMs.
source: in 'half-crush' injuries, puc-lacZ is induced in most non-VUM MNs on the side of the crush, but is not induced in VUMs.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: In Drosophila MNs, Wnd signaling is not tuned to detect axonal damage per se, but is instead uniquely tuned to detect a complete loss of innervation.
source: These combined observations suggest that in Drosophila MNs, Wnd signaling is not tuned to detect axonal damage per se, but is instead uniquely tuned to detect a complete loss of innervation, which occurs following some injuries but not others.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: A total of 22 genetic manipulations expected to inhibit synaptic transmission were tested, but none led to a change in puc-lacZ expression.
source: Summarized, we tested a total of 22 genetic manipulations expected to inhibit synaptic transmission, but none led to a change in puc-lacZ expression.
evidence: This is a summary of negative results from the study.

claim: Electrical silencing of SNc MNs by Gal4/UAS-mediated expression of the Drosophila open rectifier K+ channel (dORK) did not lead to a change in puc-lacZ expression.
source: These include electrical silencing of SNc MNs by Gal4/UAS-mediated expression of the Drosophila open rectifier K+ channel (dORK) (Nitabach et al., 2002)

claim: Silencing of transmission using temperature-sensitive mutations in dynamin did not lead to a change in puc-lacZ expression.
source: silencing of transmission using temperature-sensitive mutations in dynamin (Kitamoto, 2001)

claim: Light-induced silencing of neurons expressing Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin 1 (gtACR1) did not lead to a change in puc-lacZ expression.
source: and light-induced silencing of neurons expressing Guillardia theta anion channelrhodopsin 1 (gtACR1) (Mohammad et al., 2017; Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a negative result from the study.

claim: Many genetic manipulations that perturb evoked and/or spontaneous synaptic transmission do not yield synaptic phenotypes associated with Wnd activation.
source: Consistent with these negative results, we noted that previous studies have described many genetic manipulations that perturb evoked and/or spontaneous synaptic transmission (Choi et al., 2014; Daniels et al., 2006; DiAntonio and Schwarz, 1994; Han et al., 2022; Kim et al., 2012; Mosca et al., 2005; Pittendrigh et al., 1997) do not yield synaptic phenotypes (of synaptic overgrowth or decreased VGlut expression levels) associated with Wnd activation (Collins et al., 2006; Li et al., 2017).

claim: PHR localizes to synaptic terminals.
source: PHR is an attractive candidate since it localizes to synaptic terminals (Abrams et al., 2008; Opperman and Grill, 2014; Zhen et al., 2000)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Loss of PHR function leads to increased levels of Wnd/DLK at synapses.
source: and loss of PHR function leads to increased levels of Wnd/DLK at synapses (Collins et al., 2006; Nakata et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Uninjured MNSNc neurons in male hiwΔN mutants have an increased number of axon collateral and terminal branches at muscles 26, 29, and 27 NMJs.
source: Consistent with previously reported phenotypes for hiw in other MN types (Collins et al., 2006; Wan et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2005), uninjured MNSNc neurons in male hiwΔN mutants have an increased number of axon collateral and terminal branches at muscles 26, 29, and 27 NMJs (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with previous observations, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Uninjured neurons show elevated expression of puc-lacZ in hiwΔN mutants compared to control animals.
source: Also consistent with previous observations, uninjured neurons show elevated expression of puc-lacZ in hiwΔN mutants compared to control animals (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, consistent with previous observations, shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Injuries that removed all synaptic terminals led to an even further elevation of puc-lacZ expression in hiwΔN mutant neurons.
source: Strikingly, injuries that removed all synaptic terminals led to an even further elevation of puc-lacZ expression in hiwΔN mutant neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: Laser axotomies that removed all synaptic branches from either MNSNc-26/29 and/or MNSNc-27 neurons led to further elevation of puc-lacZ in hiwΔN mutants.
source: This was the case for laser axotomies that removed all synaptic branches from either MNSNc-26/29 and/or MNSNc-27 neurons (Figure 3A, right column, and Figure 3B)
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3B.

claim: VUM neurons following nerve crush injuries showed further elevation of puc-lacZ in hiwΔN mutants.
source: and also for VUM neurons following nerve crush injuries (Figure 3C)

claim: Injuries to a single synaptic branch (on muscle 29) of MNSNc-26/29 in hiwΔN mutants had a similar level of puc-lacZ expression as uninjured hiwΔN neurons.
source: Injuries to a single synaptic branch (on muscle 29) of MNSNc-26/29 in hiwΔN mutants had a similar level of puc-lacZ expression as uninjured hiwΔN neurons (Figure 3A, B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 3A, B.

claim: The presence of a spared synapse is capable of restraining Wnd signaling independently of Hiw's function.
source: Collectively, these observations suggest that the presence of a spared synapse is capable of restraining Wnd signaling independently of Hiw's function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The ability of injured neurons to degenerate and regenerate their axons facilitates nervous system repair.
source: The intrinsic ability of injured neurons to degenerate and regenerate their axons facilitates nervous system repair
evidence: This is a general statement about nervous system repair.

claim: The ability of neurons to degenerate and regenerate their axons is not engaged in all neurons and injury locations.
source: however, this ability is not engaged in all neurons and injury locations

claim: For C. elegans PLM mechanosensory neurons, robust regeneration occurs following injuries that remove both the synaptic and sensory branches.
source: For C. elegans PLM mechanosensory neurons, robust regeneration occurs following injuries that remove both the synaptic and sensory branches, but not following injuries that leave a synaptic branch intact (Wu et al., 2007).

claim: For C. elegans PLM mechanosensory neurons, robust regeneration does not occur following injuries that leave a synaptic branch intact.
source: For C. elegans PLM mechanosensory neurons, robust regeneration occurs following injuries that remove both the synaptic and sensory branches, but not following injuries that leave a synaptic branch intact (Wu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: In the mammalian spinal cord, remarkable regeneration occurred following injuries proximal to the branching point of sensory neurons (which led to removal of all branches).
source: In the mammalian spinal cord, an elegant study following responses to laser-induced microsurgery to ascending and descending central projections of sensory neurons observed that remarkable regeneration occurred following injuries proximal to the branching point (which led to removal of all branches) but not distal (which left one branch intact) (Lorenzana et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: In the mammalian spinal cord, remarkable regeneration did not occur following injuries distal to the branching point of sensory neurons (which left one branch intact).
source: In the mammalian spinal cord, an elegant study following responses to laser-induced microsurgery to ascending and descending central projections of sensory neurons observed that remarkable regeneration occurred following injuries proximal to the branching point (which led to removal of all branches) but not distal (which left one branch intact) (Lorenzana et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Synaptic proteins alpha2-delta, Munc13, and RIM are implicated in restraining regenerative ability of axons in mice.
source: Studies in mice have also implicated synaptic proteins alpha2-delta, Munc13, and RIM in restraining regenerative ability of axons (Hilton et al., 2022; Tedeschi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Spared afferent synaptic connections that remain following injuries distal to the branch point may inhibit the regeneration ability of centrally projecting axons in the spinal cord.
source: These observations are consistent with the possibility that spared afferent synaptic connections that remain following injuries distal to the branch point inhibit the regeneration ability of centrally projecting axons in the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on cited studies.

claim: Many of the axons that project over great distances in the spinal cord have at least one synaptic branch.
source: It is noteworthy that many of the axons that project over great distances in the spinal cord have at least one synaptic branch.
evidence: This is a general statement about spinal cord anatomy.

claim: Neurons that project through the corticospinal tract (CST) form synaptic branches in the red nucleus, brainstem, and throughout the spinal cord.
source: Neurons that project through the corticospinal tract (CST), whose poor regeneration ability following spinal cord injury is most widely studied, form synaptic branches in the red nucleus, brainstem, and throughout the spinal cord (Raineteau and Schwab, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: Regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) and phosphorylated cJun are not induced in CST neurons following spinal cord injury.
source: Strikingly, regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) and phosphorylated cJun, a marker of DLK signaling activation, are not induced in CST neurons following spinal cord injury but are robustly induced following intracortical injuries close to CST cell bodies (Mason et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) and phosphorylated cJun are robustly induced in CST neurons following intracortical injuries close to CST cell bodies.
source: Strikingly, regeneration-associated genes (RAGs) and phosphorylated cJun, a marker of DLK signaling activation, are not induced in CST neurons following spinal cord injury but are robustly induced following intracortical injuries close to CST cell bodies (Mason et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Restraint of DLK signaling activation by spared synaptic branches could be a prominent feature of the poor intrinsic regeneration capacity of neurons following spinal cord injury.
source: Since the latter may be the only form of injury that removes all synaptic branches from the CST neurons, we propose that restraint of DLK signaling activation by spared synaptic branches could be a prominent feature of the poor intrinsic regeneration capacity of neurons following spinal cord injury.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation based on the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: Genetic manipulations that inhibit or perturb synaptic transmission and/or neuronal excitability did not reveal a requirement for synaptic transmission in the restraint of Wnd by spared synaptic branches.
source: Using genetic manipulations that inhibit or perturb synaptic transmission and/or neuronal excitability, we did not detect a requirement for synaptic transmission in the restraint of Wnd by spared synaptic branches.
evidence: This is a summary of negative results from the study.

claim: Studies in multiple model organisms have shown that loss of PHR leads to increased levels of Wnd/DLK in axons.
source: The PHR ubiquitin ligase, known as Hiw in Drosophila, was a logical candidate to regulate Wnd at synapses, since studies in multiple model organisms have shown that loss of this enzyme leads to increased levels of Wnd/DLK in axons (Collins et al., 2006; Huntwork-Rodriguez et al., 2013; Nakata et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: The puc-lacZ reporter implies that Wnd signaling is elevated in hiw mutants.
source: The puc-lacZ reporter implies that Wnd signaling is elevated in hiw mutants.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's data.

claim: The restraint conferred by spared synaptic branches is still active in the absence of Hiw.
source: However, the restraint conferred by spared synaptic branches is still active in the absence of Hiw, since Wnd signaling can be further elevated by axotomy of all synapses in hiw null mutants (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study, shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nerve crush injury led to a rapid down-regulation of an ectopically expressed Hiw-GFP transgene.
source: In a previous study, we noted that the nerve crush injury led to a rapid down-regulation of an ectopically expressed Hiw-GFP transgene and speculated that impairment of restraint by Hiw leads to activation of Wnd signaling in injured axons (Xiong et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors.

claim: The current data suggest the existence of additional mechanisms that restrain Wnd signaling at intact synapses beyond Hiw.
source: Our current data do not rule out a role for Hiw but suggest the existence of additional mechanisms that restrain Wnd signaling at intact synapses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Hiw-independent downregulation of Wnd protein occurs concomitantly with the development of presynaptic boutons in photoreceptor growth cone termination.
source: This has also been suggested from developmental studies of photoreceptor growth cone termination, in which Hiw-independent downregulation of Wnd protein occurs concomitantly with the development of presynaptic boutons (Feoktistov and Herman, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a cited study.

claim: The regulation of Wnd is linked to the trafficking of organelles between the synaptic terminal and cell body, akin to neurotrophin signaling.
source: We speculate that the regulation of Wnd is linked to the trafficking of organelles between the synaptic terminal and cell body, akin to neurotrophin signaling, which relies on retrograde trafficking of signaling endosomes in axons (Cosker et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: DLK signaling becomes activated following nerve growth factor withdrawal from distal axons.
source: Consistent with this idea, DLK signaling becomes activated following nerve growth factor withdrawal from distal axons (Ghosh et al., 2011; Larhammar et al., 2017).

claim: Previous studies of Wnd signaling have documented its dependence on retrograde axonal transport machinery.
source: Previous studies of Wnd signaling have documented its dependence on retrograde axonal transport machinery (Xiong et al., 2010).

claim: Mutations that disrupt axonal cytoskeleton and the unc-104/kif1A kinesin lead to Wnd/DLK signaling activation.
source: Moreover, mutations that disrupt axonal cytoskeleton and the unc-104/kif1A kinesin also lead to Wnd/DLK signaling activation (Li et al., 2017; Valakh et al., 2015; Valakh et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Both Wnd and its homologue DLK in mice show regulated association with organelle membranes via palmitoylation.
source: Both Wnd and its homologue DLK in mice show regulated association with organelle membranes via palmitoylation, and disruption of its palmitoylation abolishes DLK's signaling ability (Holland et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

claim: Disruption of DLK palmitoylation abolishes DLK's signaling ability.
source: Both Wnd and its homologue DLK in mice show regulated association with organelle membranes via palmitoylation, and disruption of its palmitoylation abolishes DLK's signaling ability (Holland et al., 2016; Kim et al., 2024; Niu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by cited studies.

source: Consistent with this idea, a recent study has shown that Wnd signaling can be ectopically activated in the cell body when its transport to distal synapses is impaired in rab11 mutants (Kim et al., 2024).

claim: DLK/Wnd must be tightly regulated both at synapses and cell bodies.
source: Given the many factors that have been documented thus far that regulate DLK/Wnd protein or signaling (Asghari Adib et al., 2018), we think that this kinase must be tightly regulated both at synapses and cell bodies (Figure 4).

claim: Regulation at both synapses and cell bodies gives the neuron a way to monitor the state of its entire axon and restrict signaling activation to scenarios where all efferent connections of the axon are disrupted.
source: Regulation at both locations gives the neuron a way to monitor the state of its entire axon and restrict signaling activation to scenarios where all efferent connections of the axon are disrupted.

source: Previous studies using this reporter line have shown that expression of nuclear localized lacZ is strongly induced following nerve injury, requiring Wnd, JNK, and the Fos transcription factor (Xiong et al., 2010).
